there is a statistically significant increased risk of cancer in paper and pulp industry workers.

“Pulping and paper making processes generate a large number of organic compounds, many of which are toxic, but the occupational exposures are generally low and the cancer risks are limited to a few cancer sites”.
In the pulp and paper industry, there are increased risks for cancers of the lymphatic, haematopoietetic and stomach systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
occupational exposures and health effects in the pulp and wood processing industries.
the development of a job-exposure-matrix for the paper and pulp industries, which will enable us to identify and quantify the exposure of paper and pulp mill workers to various chemical compounds.
the identification of occupational and environmental carcinogens and their effects in the pulp and wood industries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a lack of knowledge of the cancer risk among pulp and paper workers.
the evidence of carcinogenicity in the pulp and wood industries is inconclusive.
there is a need for further epidemiological studies, and that there is no clear evidence for a carcinogenic effect from pulp and paper industry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk for lung cancer is increased in the pulp and board mill industries, and that there is a possible risk for stomach cancer in the paper industries.
there are no conclusive findings of carcinogenic risks for the pulp and paper industry.
the pulp and paper workers are exposed to a mixture of substances that have not yet been identified as carcinogenic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pulp and paper industry is an interesting field for future epidemiological research on occupational cancer.
there is no evidence for a cancer excess for the paper and pulp industries in general, but that the industry is a heterogeneous group with respect to cancer risks.
there is a need to identify specific exposure sources and compounds in the industry, which may explain the observed excesses.
